name: Attentional bias
statement: Anxious people are said to give threatening information more of their attention than neutral information, and to be quicker to spot anything that appears where a threat was.
meaning: The claim is about where attention goes in the first half-second, not about what somebody chooses to think about. Two tasks carry almost the whole literature. In the dot probe, a threat word or face and a neutral one appear together for a few hundred milliseconds, then a probe replaces one of them and the participant presses a key. Responses are compared between trials where the probe replaced the threat and trials where it replaced the neutral item, and the difference in milliseconds is the bias index. In the emotional Stroop, threat words are colour-named and the extra time they cost is the index. Both indices are difference scores, and both are usually treated as a property of the person rather than of the trial. The clinical version of the claim is stronger than the descriptive one: that this tendency helps cause and sustain anxiety, and that reversing it should therefore reduce symptoms. That last step is what attention bias modification tries to do, and it is where the evidence divides.

origin.who: Colin MacLeod, Andrew Mathews and Philip Tata
origin.note: The paper introduced the dot probe. It could not be read for this audit, so its results are not described here. Bar-Haim and colleagues, whose 2007 review was read in full, say MacLeod and colleagues built the task to answer the objection that slow responses to threat words reflect response bias or arousal rather than attention. Because the participant responds to a neutral probe, that reading is closed off. Bar-Haim also cites the 1986 paper for the finding that non-anxious people shift attention away from mild threat.

evidence: Bar-Haim and four colleagues pooled the field in 2007. Their meta-analysis covers 172 samples in 142 journal articles, 4,031 participants, published between February 1986 and May 2005, yielding 323 effects under a random-effects model. Threat-related bias was significant within anxious participants, k = 112, n = 2,263, d = 0.45, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.49, p < .01. It was absent in non-anxious controls, k = 87, n = 1,768, d = -0.007, 95% CI -0.06 to 0.05, p = .85. The between-groups comparison gave d = 0.41, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.48. The bias held for subliminal exposures, k = 20, d = 0.32, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.44, and for supraliminal ones, k = 90, d = 0.48, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.54, with no significant difference between them. By paradigm the anxious-group figures were d = 0.49 for the emotional Stroop, k = 70, d = 0.37 for the dot probe, k = 35, and d = 0.43 for emotional spatial cuing, k = 7. Among clinically diagnosed participants specifically, the dot-probe estimate was d = 0.34, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.46, k = 16. Blocked emotional Stroop designs gave d = 0.69, k = 31, against d = 0.35 for randomised designs, k = 30. Blocked designs were the one condition in which controls showed any bias, d = 0.21, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.31. The authors calculate that the anxious-group result could not be reduced to insignificance by the next 11,339 null studies. On the treatment side, Hakamata and seven colleagues pooled 12 randomised trials of attention bias modification from 10 publications, 467 participants, searched in MEDLINE from January 1995 to February 2010. The accepted manuscript, which is the version open at PubMed Central, reports a medium effect on anxiety, d = 0.61, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.81, p < .001, with a fail-safe N of 54. PubMed's record prints that figure as d = .51, marked as corrected, and lists an erratum at Biological Psychiatry 2012, volume 72, issue 5, page 429. The manuscript's own sensitivity check cuts as deep as the erratum does. Dropping the three trials with the largest effects leaves d = 0.36, k = 9, 372 participants, and a fail-safe N of 7. The effect on the bias index itself was large, d = 1.16, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.50, but it rests on seven of the twelve trials and 207 participants, none of them patients. Only three of the 12 trials used anxiety-disorder patients, and none used children.

examples.text: Someone with social anxiety walks into a room and their eye lands on the person who looks unimpressed before they have taken in anyone else. Nothing was decided. The look had already gone there by the time the room registered.

examples.tag: Dog-shaped at the end of the street
examples.text: A person afraid of dogs picks out the dog before they pick out the car or the person holding the lead. A walker with no fear of dogs shows almost none of this, which is why the claim is about anxious attention rather than about attention.

examples.tag: Losing the line on the page
examples.text: A health-anxious reader working through a leaflet finds their eye pulled to a frightening word and has to find their place again. The cost is the fraction of a second it took, and it is measured in exactly that.

replication.headline: Bar-Haim's meta-analysis puts dot-probe bias in clinically anxious people at d = 0.34; pooling the baseline measures of 1,005 diagnosed patients in treatment trials puts it at 1.8 milliseconds, d = .05.
replication.detail: Kruijt, Parsons and Fox went to a body of data collected for another purpose. Attention bias modification trials measure the dot-probe bias index before training starts, and those baseline measures had never been pooled. Across 13 randomised trials and 1,005 clinically diagnosed anxious and post-traumatic-stress patients, the random-effects mean bias index was 1.8 ms, SE 1.26 ms, 95% CI -0.6 to 4.3, p = .144, which they report as d = .05. A Bayes factor of .23 favoured the point-zero hypothesis, and an interval analysis put the mean bias in the 0 to 5 ms range with a Bayes factor of 369.1. Their samples ranged from 7 to 134 people with a median of 82, which they call four times the sample size of about 20 commonly used to compare bias between clinical and control groups. Bar-Haim's clinical dot-probe estimate rested on 302 anxious participants across 16 studies, so the new pooling holds about three times as many. Because the measures were taken as trial baselines rather than as findings, publication bias has less purchase on them. The two results are not straightforwardly reconcilable, and the authors say it should no longer be assumed that clinically anxious people are characterised by attention towards threat. The treatment literature splits the same way. Mogoaşe, David and Koster included 43 controlled trials, 2,268 participants and 47 group comparisons. Their symptom analysis drew on 42 of those comparisons and 1,979 participants, giving g = 0.196, 95% CI 0.085 to 0.308. Dropping two outlying comparisons produced the g = 0.160, 95% CI 0.055 to 0.265, that the abstract prints. The anxiety subset was g = 0.260, 95% CI 0.132 to 0.388, and no other symptom category showed a significant effect after training. Cristea, Kok and Cuijpers pooled 49 randomised trials of cognitive bias modification, 22 comparisons training attention and 23 training interpretation. Among the clinically diagnosed samples, anxiety across all measures gave g = 0.28, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.55, and removing one outlier left a non-significant g = 0.16. Effects fell again after adjustment for publication bias, and their meta-regression put interpretation training above attention training for anxiety and for depression. Entry 310 carries that half of the evidence. Eleven of the 49 trials tested formally whether symptom change ran through bias change, and four of those reported clear evidence that it did.

study.cite: Kruijt, A.-W., Parsons, S., & Fox, E. (2019). A meta-analysis of bias at baseline in RCTs of attention bias modification: No evidence for dot-probe bias towards threat in clinical anxiety and PTSD. Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 128(6), 563-573.

limits: The measurement is the weak point, and it has been known to be weak since 2005. Schmukle ran two studies of the dot probe, one with words and one with pictures, and his abstract concludes that estimates of internal consistency and one-week retest reliability make the task 'a completely unreliable measure of attentional allocation in non-clinical samples'. That abstract was read as the publisher deposited it with Crossref. The article itself was not obtained, so no coefficients from it are quoted here. Rodebaugh and seven colleagues found the same in a clinical sample: 24 people with a current anxiety disorder, two dot-probe sessions about three weeks apart, 1,216 trials. The global bias score returned internal consistencies of -.32 and -.48 across the two visits, split-half correlations of -.38 and -.06, and a test-retest ICC across all trials of -.36, 95% CI -.70 to .06. Negative reliabilities of that kind mean the test's assumptions have failed, not that the measure runs backwards. They reviewed the 13 studies they could find that report this reliability, and say most of them show it to be unacceptable. Two carry that result across stimulus durations, clinical and non-clinical samples, and words against pictures. Six others found reliability that might pass, though three of the six reached it only by departing from standard practice. Scores built from the timing of individual trials rather than from a condition average did better in their data. Internal consistencies ran from .77 to .97 and retest ICCs reached .90, but the two peak indices were the weak ones, with retest ICCs below .50. MacLeod, Grafton and Notebaert draw the distinction that matters. Groups high in anxiety vulnerability do on average show elevated attention to threat, and the existing tasks can separate groups. The same tasks lack the internal consistency and retest reliability needed to classify one person, and the authors judge that individuals are unlikely each to carry a stable, invariant bias. That claim about people is different from a claim about instruments, and the difference decides what the task may be used for. The colour-word Stroop effect has the same shape of problem and is entry 72. Nothing here covers attentional bias to alcohol, drug or food cues, which is a separate literature that was not searched for this entry.
misreadings: The commonest error is treating a bias index as a trait score. A difference between two condition means, each estimated from a few hundred noisy reaction times, ranks people badly even when the average effect is real, and the reliability figures above are what that looks like. A dot-probe score is therefore a poor input to any study correlating attention with symptoms, brain measures or treatment response, which is most of what the score has been used for. The second error is reading the 2007 meta-analysis as a finding about people in general. It is not: non-anxious controls showed d = -0.007, and Bar-Haim and colleagues note that this sits awkwardly with the claim that humans are wired to orient towards threat. The one exception was the blocked emotional Stroop, where controls did show a small bias. The third error concerns the participant counts. Bar-Haim's paper gives 4,031 participants in total, which is what the two within-group analyses hold between them, while the between-groups analyses use 2,963 anxious and 2,906 control participants, and Kruijt and colleagues describe the same meta-analysis as totalling 5,869 people. The figures count overlapping sets, and quoting one as the study's sample size misstates it. Fourth, attention bias modification is often cited as an established treatment on the strength of the 2010 meta-analysis. That analysis rested on 12 trials, three of them in patients, and its headline effect was corrected downwards after publication. Its own authors also reported that dropping the three largest trials cut it to d = 0.36. Later and larger pools put the symptom benefit between g = 0.16 and g = 0.20, and at nothing in the clinically diagnosed samples once outliers and publication bias are accounted for. Last, a null result on the dot probe is not proof that anxious attention is ordinary. An unreliable instrument cannot establish absence any more than it can establish presence, which is why the 1,005-patient baseline pooling matters: it is large enough that the measurement noise averages out.
